screens.title: Arduino Setup and C Programming for IoT
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson we will take a practical path from installing the Arduino IDE to writing C-style sketches that power simple Internet of Things prototypes. You will learn how the Arduino programming model uses two required functions, one that runs once to initialize hardware and one that repeats forever to read sensors and act on the world. We will also cover data types and control structures that matter because Arduino devices have limited memory, and you'll see how the Serial library becomes your primary debugging and communication tool. By the end you will be able to write a small sketch that reads a sensor, prints structured data, and accepts simple serial commands from a connected gateway. Along the way we call out a common mistake — choosing the wrong board or serial port — and show why it breaks uploads and serial monitoring. Think of this chapter as the practical toolkit for turning sensors and LEDs into connected IoT behavior. Ready to begin building repeatable, debuggable sketches that communicate with a gateway?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Arduino Setup and C
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Arduino Setup and C Programming for IoT

Install the IDE, understand board and port selection, and write sketches that initialize sensors, read data, and communicate over serial. This chapter focuses on practical, repeatable patterns for IoT prototypes.

In this lesson
You will set up the Arduino IDE, view the blink example, write a sensor-reading sketch, and use the Serial Monitor to send and receive simple commands.
Why it matters
Small boards and simple code let you iterate quickly. Understanding setup, loop and serial saves time when your prototype must report sensor data reliably.
Explore Key Topics
IDE & Boards — configure board and serial port to upload and debug.
Sketch Structure — how setup runs once and loop repeats indefinitely.
Serial I/O — send readings and accept simple commands for remote control.
Visual concept
IDE & Upload
Select board and serial port, open the Serial Monitor to see output and type commands back to the board.
Sketch Lifecycle
setup() runs once. loop() repeats. Use setup to configure pins and Serial; use loop to read sensors and send data.
Data Types
Choose int, float, or byte carefully. Memory on small Arduinos is limited to a few kilobytes.
Serial Protocols
Send CSV or JSON for structured parsing. Use Serial.available() before reading to avoid errors.
Starter example
void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(13, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  digitalWrite(13, HIGH);
  delay(1000);
  digitalWrite(13, LOW);
  delay(1000);
}

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives orient the skills you'll practice. First, you will install and configure the Arduino IDE and learn board selection and port configuration so that uploads and serial monitoring work reliably. A common error is choosing the wrong board or port; correcting that early saves time. Second, you will write sketches in Arduino's C-like language using variables, control structures, functions and arrays so your device can sense, decide, and act. Skilled use of these constructs keeps your code maintainable and efficient on small hardware. Third, you will explain and apply the required sketch structure: setup runs once to initialize hardware and loop repeats forever to implement the device behavior. Understanding this pattern helps you design cyclic sampling and low-power routines. Fourth, you will use the Serial Monitor for debugging and communication: print sensor values, format structured records for a gateway, and parse incoming simple commands. Practicing these skills will let you prototype a temperature logger that reports to a gateway and accepts remote commands to change sampling rates.

screens.title: What is an Arduino and why use it for IoT?
screens.narratorSegment: An Arduino is an open-source electronics platform combining a small microcontroller board with an easy-to-use programming environment. Its simplicity, low cost, and large ecosystem of shields and libraries make it the workhorse for early IoT prototypes. For example, if you want to measure a temperature and send it to a gateway, you’ll often choose an Arduino to read the sensor, perform a small calculation, and emit the result over a serial link. The platform trades complex operating system features for immediate access to pins, timers, and serial interfaces. That trade is useful: you get deterministic control over sensors and actuators and the ability to iterate quickly on hardware. A common misconception is that Arduinos are only for hobbyists. In reality, they form the rapid-prototyping layer of many production designs and are ideal for testing communication patterns before scaling. Remember that memory is limited on many Arduino models — for instance, an Uno has only about two kilobytes of SRAM — so keep data structures tight and prefer efficient types when you store sensor data. How will you use that constraint to shape your next prototype?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Arduino is a simple, open microcontroller platform ideal for quick IoT prototyping and learning hardware-software integration.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › What is an Arduino?
Definition
Open microcontroller platform for hardware prototyping

Designed for low-cost, accessible control of sensors, actuators, and simple communications. Ideal for testing IoT data flows before moving to gateways or cloud integrations.

Analogy
Think of Arduino as the microcontroller's training wheels: it exposes pins and simple APIs so you can focus on behavior instead of OS details.
Concrete example
Use an Arduino Uno to read a temperature sensor and send CSV-formatted readings over USB to a Raspberry Pi for logging.
Key Takeaway

Arduino gives you fast access to hardware and a simple programming model, making it ideal for iterating IoT prototypes.

Platform details
The board exposes digital and analog pins, PWM outputs, timers, and serial ports. Libraries provide sensor drivers and communication helpers so you do not rewrite low-level code.
Strength
Quick hardware access and large community examples.
Constraint
Limited RAM and no full OS — choose data structures carefully.
Why it matters
Because IoT prototypes must be simple, reliable, and resource-aware, the Arduino's trade-offs let you prototype communication and sensor handling quickly.

screens.title: The setup() and loop() lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: Every Arduino sketch follows a predictable lifecycle: setup runs once at start, then loop runs continuously. Setup is where you configure pin modes, begin Serial communication, and initialize sensor libraries. Loop contains the main behavior: reading sensors, processing data, acting on outputs, and communicating. In IoT designs the loop often follows a read-process-send-sleep pattern. For instance, a temperature logger might read a sensor every ten seconds, store recent values in an array for averaging, and then send a summarized message to a gateway once per minute. It might then enter a low-activity wait or delay until the next cycle. One common pitfall is putting long blocking code directly in setup or loop without considering responsiveness; for example, long delays or blocking network calls can make the sketch unresponsive to commands. Use non-blocking techniques or smaller delay windows when you need to accept serial commands. Understanding this lifecycle helps you structure sketches so they are predictable, testable, and able to integrate with external controllers that interact via serial or other links. What sampling pattern will you design for your next sensor?

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle pattern
keyIdea.text: Use setup for initialization and loop for repeated read-process-send cycles; avoid blocking code to remain responsive to serial commands.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › setup() and loop()
Pattern
Read → Process → Send → Wait

Use setup to start Serial and configure pins. Use loop to implement periodic sensor reads, simple processing such as averaging, and communication to a gateway.

Non-blocking tip
Avoid long blocking delays if you need to respond to serial commands. Consider state timers or shorter sleep intervals to poll for input.
Common mistake
Placing heavy processing in setup so that loop never has a chance to run as intended, or using large delays that block serial parsing.
Example: temperature logger
Read sensor every 10 seconds, push value into an array of five samples, compute average, and send average to the gateway once a minute. Then continue sampling. This balances local smoothing with less frequent transmissions to save bandwidth.
Check your understanding
  • Why use setup() for pinMode and Serial.begin?
  • How does averaging reduce noisy sensor readings?
  • When might a short delay be acceptable?
Key Takeaway

Structure code around initialization and repeatable cycles; plan for responsiveness when accepting serial commands.

screens.title: The Blink sketch: upload, run, and iterate
screens.narratorSegment: The Blink example is the canonical first test. It confirms your IDE installation, board selection, and upload path. The sketch initializes pin 13 as an output and toggles it on and off with one second delays. Running Blink verifies that the bootloader and upload settings are correct and that the board can execute code. When you modify the sketch, observe both the upload log and the board behavior: if nothing changes, recheck the board type and serial port selection, which is the most common setup error. Use the Serial Monitor for later experiments, but Blink itself uses digitalWrite and delay for a visible LED test. After successfully running Blink, try shortening the delays or moving the LED control into a function to practice refactoring. This helps you confirm you can edit, recompile, and upload reliably. Finally, use Blink as a calibration point: if a later sketch fails to upload or behave correctly, verify that Blink still works to rule out hardware issues. The Blink sketch: upload, run, and iterate means blink is the simplest verification that your ide, board, and upload process are working; use it before progressing to sensors and serial i/o.. In practical terms, step through the classic example to confirm ide and board setup. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Blink walkthrough
Editor
void setup() {
  // Initialize serial communication at 9600 baud
  Serial.begin(9600);
  // Configure pin 13 as an output
  pinMode(13, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  // Turn the LED on
  digitalWrite(13, HIGH);
  // Wait 1 second
  delay(1000);
  // Turn the LED off
  digitalWrite(13, LOW);
  // Wait 1 second
  delay(1000);
}
This example demonstrates initialization and a simple repeating action. Use it to verify uploads and experiment with timing and refactoring into functions.
Walkthrough
  • setup: begin Serial and set pin mode.
  • loop: alternate HIGH and LOW with delay to blink LED.
  • Modify timing or move code into named functions to practice structure.
Troubleshooting tip
If upload fails, check board and serial port selection first; if the board does not blink, re-upload Blink to confirm hardware health.
Key Takeaway

Run Blink as your first verification step. It isolates IDE, port, and board issues before you add sensors or networking.

screens.title: Reading sensors and transforming data
screens.narratorSegment: Reading a sensor on Arduino begins with analogRead, which returns a raw integer value that you transform into engineering units. For a typical 10‑bit ADC on many Arduinos, analogRead returns values from 0 to 1023. To convert that into voltage you multiply by the reference voltage divided by ADC resolution. For example, voltage equals sensorValue times 5.0 divided by 1023.0. That transforms raw counts into a human-friendly voltage number. In IoT applications you often collect several samples and compute an average to smooth noise. For example, sample every ten seconds and maintain the last five readings in an array to compute an average before sending. Keep memory in mind: arrays consume SRAM, so size them conservatively on devices with limited R A M. Also pick data types carefully: use int or byte where appropriate, and float only when necessary due to larger footprint. After computing and possibly formatting as CSV or JSON, send the string over Serial to the gateway. This sequence — read, transform, buffer, format, send — is the basic data pipeline for many Arduino-based IoT sensors. Reading sensors and transforming data means transform raw adc values into voltages and engineering units, buffer samples for averaging, and format for serial transmission while being mindful of memory.. In practical terms, from analogread to meaningful values and averaging. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Sensor pipeline
keyIdea.text: Transform raw ADC values into voltages and engineering units, buffer samples for averaging, and format for serial transmission while being mindful of memory.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Sensor reading
Transform
Use the ADC value and known reference to compute voltage or temperature with simple arithmetic. Be explicit about the divisor to preserve precision.
int sensorValue = analogRead(A0);
float voltage = sensorValue * (5.0 / 1023.0);
Serial.print("Sensor: ");
Serial.print(sensorValue);
Serial.print("  Voltage: ");
Serial.println(voltage);
delay(1000);
Averaging with arrays
Store recent samples in a small array, compute the average before sending. Arrays use SRAM, so pick a small buffer size on an Uno.
Example flow
  1. Read ADC using analogRead.
  2. Convert counts to voltage or temperature.
  3. Push value into a circular buffer for averaging.
  4. Format as CSV or JSON and send over Serial.
Memory note
Arduino Uno has limited SRAM (about 2 KB); avoid large arrays or many String objects to prevent fragmentation or crashes.
Key Takeaway

Transform raw readings into useful units and manage buffering and formats with memory constraints in mind.

screens.title: Variables and data types in Arduino C/C++
screens.narratorSegment: Arduino programming uses C and C++ data types. The common types you will use include int for integers, float for decimal numbers, char for single characters, boolean for true/false, long for larger integers, unsigned int and byte for small unsigned numbers. Choosing the right type matters because Arduinos have limited R A M and program memory. For example, using float where int suffices wastes space and computation time. Use byte or unsigned int for small counters or flags, and reserve floats for sensor calibration or voltage conversion when fractional precision is required. Arrays of floats multiply memory quickly, so prefer integer scaling if you can, such as storing millivolts as integers instead of volts as floats. Keep in mind that the Uno uses 2 KB of SRAM, so a modest number of float arrays can exhaust memory. A common misconception is that higher-level constructs like Strings are always fine. In embedded contexts, String objects can fragment memory over time; prefer C-style char buffers or careful use of fixed-size buffers for serial formatting to avoid fragmentation. Variables and data types in Arduino C/C++ means pick the smallest appropriate data type to save ram; avoid heavy use of floats and string objects on small arduino boards.. In practical terms, choose types carefully for memory-constrained iot devices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Variables & data types
Common types
  • int — integer numbers for general use.
  • float — decimal numbers, use sparingly.
  • byte / unsigned int — small positive values, memory efficient.
  • char — single characters; C-style strings use char arrays.
Memory practice
Prefer scaled integers over floats when possible. For example, store millivolts as integers instead of volts as floats to save RAM.
Key Takeaway

Matching types to data keeps memory usage low and code responsive on small microcontrollers.

Concrete example
A temperature stored as an int in tenths of degrees avoids using a float array. For a 2 KB SRAM board, that difference matters when you buffer samples.
Misconception
String objects are convenient but can fragment heap memory over time. Use fixed-size char arrays when you format repeated serial messages.
Quick reference
  • Use byte for small counts.
  • Use long for timestamps if needed.
  • Minimize float arrays on small Arduinos.

screens.title: Control structures: when to use if, for, and while
screens.narratorSegment: Control structures let your Arduino decide and repeat actions. Use if, else if, and else for conditional decisions — for example, if a temperature exceeds a threshold, turn on a fan. Use for loops when you know how many iterations you need, such as iterating over an array of five recent samples to compute an average. Use while loops for indefinite repetition that depends on a condition, but be cautious: a long-running while loop can block serial parsing and make the device unresponsive. The difference matters in IoT because you often must read sensors, maintain responsiveness to remote commands, and schedule transmissions. A common mistake is using nested blocking loops that prevent Serial. available checks from running. Prefer structured loops with short iterations and place periodic checks for serial input inside them, or use non-blocking timing with millis-based scheduling to alternate behavior without blocking. Understanding the trade-offs between clear blocking code and responsive, non-blocking patterns will help you design robust IoT sketches. Control structures: when to use if, for, and while means use conditional statements for decisions, for loops for fixed iterations, and avoid blocking while loops that prevent serial responsiveness.. In practical terms, decisions and repetition for iot tasks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Control trade-offs
keyIdea.text: Use conditional statements for decisions, for loops for fixed iterations, and avoid blocking while loops that prevent serial responsiveness.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Control structures
If / else
Use for branching logic based on sensor values or command input. Example: if temperature > threshold then activate fan.
For loop
Use when you know the number of iterations, for instance iterating over a small buffer to compute an average.
While loop
Use with caution. While can block program flow if the exit condition depends on slow events or absent serial input.
Concrete example
Use a for loop to sum the last five samples stored in an array then divide to compute the average. Inside a timeout window, check Serial.available to allow remote commands to interrupt long operations.
Common mistake

screens.title: Strings and memory: char arrays vs String objects
screens.narratorSegment: Arduino supports two common string approaches: C-style char arrays and the String object. Char arrays are fixed-size buffers where you manage characters directly; they are memory-predictable and avoid heap fragmentation. String objects are convenient because they behave like higher-level strings, but they allocate and free memory on the heap as you manipulate them. On memory-constrained devices like the Uno, frequent concatenation and reallocation of String objects can fragment the heap and eventually cause unexpected behavior or crashes. For stable long-running IoT sketches that repeatedly format messages for Serial output, prefer a fixed char buffer and use functions like snprintf to format text safely. If you must use String, limit dynamic operations and test long-running behavior under realistic workloads. A helpful practice is to monitor available memory during development and prefer deterministic, static allocations for buffers used in serial input and output and parsing. This reduces surprises in deployed prototypes that run for hours or days. screens.title: Using the Serial library and parsing commands
screens.narratorSegment: The Serial library is the primary method to send and receive textual data between an Arduino and a host. Begin with Serial. begin in setup to set the baud rate. Use Serial. print to send data without a newline and Serial. println to send a line-terminated string. When formatting sensor readings for a gateway, choose CSV or JSON so the receiver can parse the values reliably. On the input side, always check Serial. available before reading; this tells you how many bytes are waiting in the buffer. For simple commands, read a line until newline, trim whitespace, and compare the string to known commands such as READ, LED_ON, or LED_OFF. This pattern allows a Raspberry Pi or PC to remotely request sensor values or toggle outputs. A frequent mistake is reading serial data without available checks, which can cause unpredictable reads or blocking. Finally, test both sending and receiving in the Serial Monitor: type commands and watch the Arduino respond, and observe structured output arriving from the board. This two-way channel is essential for debugging and remote control during IoT development.

content.html:

Output

int sensorValue = analogRead(A0);
float voltage = sensorValue * (5.0 / 1023.0);
Serial.print("Sensor: ");
Serial.print(sensorValue);
Serial.print("  Voltage: ");
Serial.println(voltage);
Use println when you want a newline-terminated record and print when you want to continue on the same line for structured formatting.
Parsing input
if (Serial.available() > 0) {
  String command = Serial.readStringUntil('
');
  command.trim();
  if (command == "READ") {
    int val = analogRead(A0);
    Serial.println(val);
  } else if (command == "LED_ON") {
    digitalWrite(13, HIGH);
  } else if (command == "LED_OFF") {
    digitalWrite(13, LOW);
  }
}
Best practices
Always check Serial.available before reading. Trim incoming commands and keep the protocol simple to avoid parsing errors.

Use structured output formats and safe input checks so your board and gateway can communicate reliably and avoid blocking reads.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson we will take a practical path from installing the Arduino IDE to writing C-style sketches that power simple Internet of Things prototypes. You will learn how the Arduino programming model uses two required functions, one that runs once to initialize hardware and one that repeats forever to read sensors and act on the world. We will also cover data types and control structures that matter because Arduino devices have limited memory, and you'll see how the Serial library becomes your primary debugging and communication tool. By the end you will be able to write a small sketch that reads a sensor, prints structured data, and accepts simple serial commands from a connected gateway. Along the way we call out a common mistake — choosing the wrong board or serial port — and show why it breaks uploads and serial monitoring. Think of this chapter as the practical toolkit for turning sensors and LEDs into connected IoT behavior. Ready to begin building repeatable, debuggable sketches that communicate with a gateway?

These objectives orient the skills you'll practice. First, you will install and configure the Arduino IDE and learn board selection and port configuration so that uploads and serial monitoring work reliably. A common error is choosing the wrong board or port; correcting that early saves time. Second, you will write sketches in Arduino's C-like language using variables, control structures, functions and arrays so your device can sense, decide, and act. Skilled use of these constructs keeps your code maintainable and efficient on small hardware. Third, you will explain and apply the required sketch structure: setup runs once to initialize hardware and loop repeats forever to implement the device behavior. Understanding this pattern helps you design cyclic sampling and low-power routines. Fourth, you will use the Serial Monitor for debugging and communication: print sensor values, format structured records for a gateway, and parse incoming simple commands. Practicing these skills will let you prototype a temperature logger that reports to a gateway and accepts remote commands to change sampling rates.

Now let's frame the same objectives as practical milestones you can check off. First milestone: successfully install the Arduino IDE, select the correct board and serial port, and upload the blink example. This confirms your environment is configured. Second milestone: write a sketch that reads a potentiometer and prints a voltage to the Serial Monitor every half second. This checks your understanding of analogRead, simple math with floats, and the Serial print functions. Third milestone: implement a sketch that accepts simple serial commands to change behavior, demonstrating you can parse input and control outputs remotely. Fourth milestone: refactor repeated logic into functions and, where appropriate, use arrays to store recent samples. These milestones map directly to IoT needs: reliable uploads, readable sensor output, remote control, and code organization for maintainability. Use the Serial Monitor to confirm both outgoing data and incoming commands during tests.

An Arduino is an open-source electronics platform combining a small microcontroller board with an easy-to-use programming environment. Its simplicity, low cost, and large ecosystem of shields and libraries make it the workhorse for early IoT prototypes. For example, if you want to measure a temperature and send it to a gateway, you’ll often choose an Arduino to read the sensor, perform a small calculation, and emit the result over a serial link. The platform trades complex operating system features for immediate access to pins, timers, and serial interfaces. That trade is useful: you get deterministic control over sensors and actuators and the ability to iterate quickly on hardware. A common misconception is that Arduinos are only for hobbyists. In reality, they form the rapid-prototyping layer of many production designs and are ideal for testing communication patterns before scaling. Remember that memory is limited on many Arduino models — for instance, an Uno has only about two kilobytes of SRAM — so keep data structures tight and prefer efficient types when you store sensor data. How will you use that constraint to shape your next prototype?

Every Arduino sketch follows a predictable lifecycle: setup runs once at start, then loop runs continuously. Setup is where you configure pin modes, begin Serial communication, and initialize sensor libraries. Loop contains the main behavior: reading sensors, processing data, acting on outputs, and communicating. In IoT designs the loop often follows a read-process-send-sleep pattern. For instance, a temperature logger might read a sensor every ten seconds, store recent values in an array for averaging, and then send a summarized message to a gateway once per minute. It might then enter a low-activity wait or delay until the next cycle. One common pitfall is putting long blocking code directly in setup or loop without considering responsiveness; for example, long delays or blocking network calls can make the sketch unresponsive to commands. Use non-blocking techniques or smaller delay windows when you need to accept serial commands. Understanding this lifecycle helps you structure sketches so they are predictable, testable, and able to integrate with external controllers that interact via serial or other links. What sampling pattern will you design for your next sensor?

The Blink example is the canonical first test. It confirms your IDE installation, board selection, and upload path. The sketch initializes pin 13 as an output and toggles it on and off with one second delays. Running Blink verifies that the bootloader and upload settings are correct and that the board can execute code. When you modify the sketch, observe both the upload log and the board behavior: if nothing changes, recheck the board type and serial port selection, which is the most common setup error. Use the Serial Monitor for later experiments, but Blink itself uses digitalWrite and delay for a visible LED test. After successfully running Blink, try shortening the delays or moving the LED control into a function to practice refactoring. This helps you confirm you can edit, recompile, and upload reliably. Finally, use Blink as a calibration point: if a later sketch fails to upload or behave correctly, verify that Blink still works to rule out hardware issues. The Blink sketch: upload, run, and iterate means blink is the simplest verification that your ide, board, and upload process are working; use it before progressing to sensors and serial i/o.. In practical terms, step through the classic example to confirm ide and board setup. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Reading a sensor on Arduino begins with analogRead, which returns a raw integer value that you transform into engineering units. For a typical 10‑bit ADC on many Arduinos, analogRead returns values from 0 to 1023. To convert that into voltage you multiply by the reference voltage divided by ADC resolution. For example, voltage equals sensorValue times 5.0 divided by 1023.0. That transforms raw counts into a human-friendly voltage number. In IoT applications you often collect several samples and compute an average to smooth noise. For example, sample every ten seconds and maintain the last five readings in an array to compute an average before sending. Choosing the right type matters because Arduinos have limited R A M and program memory. For example, using float where int suffices wastes space and computation time. Use byte or unsigned int for small counters or flags, and reserve floats for sensor calibration or voltage conversion when fractional precision is required.
